text: A qubit's state is a pair of complex amplitudes, but a human reading a result wants one thing: how likely is each outcome. This lesson turns amplitudes into probabilities and those probabilities into clear bar charts, the single most common plot you'll produce for the rest of this course.

A qubit measurement produces one of a fixed, discrete set of outcomes, so a bar chart, where each bar is a separate unconnected category, is the correct representation — a line plot would visually imply a relationship between zero and one that doesn't exist. abs of an amplitude squared converts a complex amplitude into a measurement probability. Fixing the y-axis to zero through one with set_ylim matters, since auto-scaling can make a genuinely large probability look small. And annotating each bar with its exact value saves a reader from estimating by eye.

For alpha equals root point three and beta equals root point seven, squaring each amplitude's magnitude gives point three and point seven, and they sum to exactly one point zero. That sum matters as much as the two individual numbers — if your computed probabilities don't sum to very close to one, the state vector wasn't normalized, and something upstream needs fixing before you ever plot it.

ax dot bar takes a sequence of category labels, zero and one, and a sequence of heights the same length, point three and point seven. Setting the y-limit explicitly to zero through one is worth doing for every probability plot you make in this course, so the scale never exaggerates or hides a real difference between runs.
Next lesson covers the Bloch sphere, the extra geometric information, relative phase, that a plain probability bar chart throws away entirely, even when two states measure identically.
